@TheEduardoRFS Pierce spending all his time on contingent details of OO while dodging any discussion of its essentials, is like studying Latin loan words and a litany of funny expressions while dodging any study of the fundamental grammar of English.

To Pierce, the point of objects is a challenge "can your types do that"? So he trains his types to do the trick, and when they do it—applause, end of the show. The point was to demonstrate type brilliance.

To me, OO is a tool that is useful because better richer and further patterns of thought we can express with it compared to without it. Types in turn can make this tool even more useful by helping us reason about those patterns, make them safer, etc. Expressing those patterns is the purpose; OO is a tool, and types are a tool for the tool. Giving simple types for the simplest OO patterns is when the type show starts in earnest, not when it ends. Going further and covering as much of the useful pattern space as possible is the point—which requires having identified that useful pattern space, and if possible its meta-pattern. Something Pierce seemingly never even bothered to think about.

@TheEduardoRFS If the purpose is to demonstrate technical brilliance, yeah, it's great to show a lot of tricks you can play to almost achieve OO while avoiding actual OO.

If the purpose is to understand and explain OO, you must confront the essence of OO head on.

TAPL is a great classic, which is why its treatment of objects deserves a great takedown: Rarely has so much technical virtuosity been expended on so elaborate a dodge.

Objects are covered in chapters 18, 19, 24, 27, 32. The presentation is clever, but long-winded and quite unsatisfactory:
§18 spends a lot of time implementing not-quite-objects, gradually adding many common but non-essential features (including imperative programming), until the reader has finally implemented actual objects with single inheritance in §18.9, §18.10... modulo the same cheat as in Pierce & Turner 1993 (the user must tie the knot manually, providing the representation type). §18.11 and §18.12 are tedious and not-so-enlightening subsets of my §5.3.2 and §6.1.5—fixpoint vs self-application models.
§19 has fake OO with no open recursion through self in types (the Jacobs dodge), i.e. the NNOOTT with enough language restrictions to make it consistent—but useless.
§24 uses existential types to abstract over representation types, but still uses the same cheat.
§27 revisits his imperative objects for more polymorphism, again a nice but secondary feature.
§32, the final chapter, returns to inheritance and open recursion between methods, and finally introduces the real thing in the very last formal section, §32.9, but without elaborating on the issues it raises. §32.10 is a collection of citations, some good, some OK, some bad (including plenty of bad Cardelli papers), and notably omitting Eifrig.

The interaction between recursive object types and inheritance is left unexplored, and the notions of mixin inheritance and multiple inheritance are barely alluded to, with the reader referred to the bibliography.
Pierce is technically masterful, but he doesn’t demonstrate any understanding of the purpose of OO—a foreign paradigm (see Gabriel 2012).
A meaningful approach would focus on the essential, even if it has to sacrifice the treatment of contingent, secondary and peripheral issues, or gloss over them—the very opposite of Pierce’s approach.

Don't get me wrong: Simula 67's classes were a landmark, and justly celebrated. But Teitelman, Bobrow & Winograd are unjustly unsung.

—But wasn't inheritance invented by Dahl & Nygaard with Simula 67?

Winograd's paper was only officially published in 1975, but the 1974 draft in Newell's archives proves the idea was already circulating early.

- Alan Kay was colleague and close friend of Bobrow, who was collaborator of Winograd on KRL. And Winograd spent half his time at PARC.

@dallaylaen Composition of mixins, or as I call them "modular extensions"—entities with a type as follows:

type ModExt inherited required newlyProvided =
  ∀ super, self : Type
    self ⊂ required self, super ⊂ inherited self ⇒
        super → self → super∩(newlyProvided self)
